questions.q: In the worked example, Northbeam's assistant costs about $3.94M/year in API calls at 2 million requests/day. Why does this number matter even though no single request is expensive?
options: Annual costs are always irrelevant compared to daily costs
A tiny per-request cost, multiplied by real production volume, becomes a large, real financial number that a prototype's low volume would never reveal
This number indicates the API pricing itself must be wrong
The cost is only theoretical and has no real budget impact
questions.explain: This is Lesson 1's 'cost' dimension made concrete -- a fraction-of-a-cent-per-request cost is invisible at small scale and becomes a board-level number once multiplied by millions of daily requests.

questions.q: Why does adding 400 tokens to a system prompt -- something that would pass a normal code review -- cost Northbeam an extra $876,000/year?
options: This number is an error -- a 400-token prompt addition cannot meaningfully affect cost
That small per-request token increase gets multiplied by 2 million requests a day, every day, turning an invisible-looking change into a large recurring cost
400 tokens always costs exactly $876,000 regardless of request volume
System prompts are billed at a different, much higher rate than other tokens
questions.explain: The same multiplication effect as the baseline cost applies to any per-request change -- a small addition that looks harmless in isolation is only harmless until you multiply it by real production volume.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a 2-second end-to-end latency target needs to be split into a budget table across each component (embedding, vector search, re-ranking, generation, network), rather than just stated as one overall goal?
options: Individual component budgets are purely a formality with no practical effect
A single overall latency number is always sufficient and never needs further detail
Without individual budgets, each team optimizes their own piece in isolation and the total can still blow the target, with no specific, measurable problem to point to
Splitting a latency target into a table always makes a system slower overall
questions.explain: A vague overall target doesn't tell any individual team what their piece needs to hit -- an explicit per-component budget table turns 'make it fast' into specific, individually enforceable numbers.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that cost and latency budgets should be set BEFORE building a system, not after?
options: Budgets set after building are always more accurate than ones set before
There is no real difference in when budgets are set -- it has no practical effect on the outcome

Fixing a budget violation after the system is already built often means a full redesign (ripping out a chosen database, renegotiating a model), while setting the constraint up front shapes the design from the start
Budgets can only be legally established after a system has launched
questions.explain: A constraint known up front shapes early design choices (e.g., which index type to pick for vector search); discovering the same constraint after launch usually means an expensive rebuild instead of a design choice.

questions.q: What is the practical reason Staff/Principal-level review happens at the design stage, according to this lesson?
options: Code review and design review always catch exactly the same set of problems
By the time code already exists, many of the expensive architectural decisions are already locked in, making design-stage review far more effective than code-review-stage review
Staff/Principal engineers are not permitted to review code after it is written
Design-stage review is purely a formality with no real influence on outcomes
questions.explain: Once code exists, foundational choices (database, model, pipeline architecture) are typically already baked in -- design-stage review is where those choices can still be changed cheaply.
